Three Famous Food Markets in Europe: Shop, Eat and Tip

Quality checked lesson

Visit three famous European food markets in Barcelona, Paris and London. Learn what you can find there, then practise the English you need to choose food, check ingredients, pay and tip.

    Need a starting line?

    Need a starting line?

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: La Boqueria sits on La Rambla in Barcelona. It has served the city as a market since 1836, and today more than 200 traders work there. Bright fruit and vegetable stalls stand beside sellers of olives and preserved foods. Visitors can also find nuts and pulses, poultry and eggs, meat, fish and seafood. Grocery stalls provide everyday ingredients, while small bars offer a place to stop and eat. This mix makes La Boqueria more than a sightseeing stop: it is a working food market where visitors can compare fresh produce, specialist foods and ready-to-eat dishes.

Text to type: Marché des Enfants Rouges is a small covered market in Paris. Founded in 1615, it is the city's oldest covered food market. Fresh produce and farm cheese share the space with counters serving ready-to-eat food. A visitor might see chicken skewers, vegetable couscous or a Breton buckwheat galette. Other choices include oysters and fresh fruit juice. The prepared food comes from several food cultures, so a short walk can reveal very different flavours. It is an easy place to choose a simple lunch while enjoying the close, historic market atmosphere.

Text to type: Borough Market has more than 100 stalls and shops in London. They are spread across Three Crown Square, Green Market and Borough Market Kitchen. Visitors can buy British seafood, regional cheese and cured meat, or stop for Middle Eastern meze, falafel or shawarma. Cakes, pastries and bao buns add quick sweet and savoury choices. The market works well for two different plans: shopping for ingredients to take home or choosing lunch and eating it nearby. Moving through its three areas shows how many kinds of food one market can bring together.

Tipping in Spain, France and the UK

between , and the . At a or , the the .

In , a is , and some the . In , , so is .

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Tipping customs change between Spain, France and the UK. At a simple market stall or self-service counter, people normally pay the displayed price unless the seller says otherwise. In Spain, a tip is optional, and some people simply round up the bill. In France, restaurant prices normally include service, so extra money is optional. In the UK, a restaurant bill may already include an optional or required service charge. A visitor should read the bill before adding more money. The safest habit in all three countries is simple: check the bill, then ask.

Roleplay 1: Shop at La Boqueria

Seller

Hello. Can I help you?

You

What is popular here?

Seller

The green olives are very popular.

You

Is this local?

Seller

Yes, these olives are from Catalonia.

You

Two hundred grams, please. I would also like two peaches. Do you take cards?

Seller

Yes, card is fine. That's six euros, please.

You

Thank you. Here are your olives and peaches.

Roleplay 2: Ask About a Nut Allergy

Cook

Hello. Would you like the rice-and-vegetable dish?

You

What is in this?

Cook

It has rice, vegetables and almonds.

You

Does this contain nuts? I am allergic to nuts.

Cook

Yes. It contains almonds, and other food here may also touch nuts.

You

Then I won't have the dish. One of these sealed waters, please.

Cook

Of course. Here you are.

You

Thank you.

Cook

You're welcome.

Your Turn: Three Market Orders

Speak through each situation. Use the phrases from the lesson.

  1. At La Boqueria, ask about local olives, order 200 grams and check card payment.

    Need a starting line?

    Start with: What is popular here?

    Helpful clue: Ask what is popular and local, give the amount, then ask whether the seller takes cards.

  2. At Marché des Enfants Rouges, ask about a dish and explain a nut allergy.

    Need a starting line?

    Start with: What is in this?

    Helpful clue: Ask about ingredients and nuts, state the allergy, then choose or refuse the food.

  3. At Borough Market, order lunch and check whether you need to add money for service.

    Need a starting line?

    Start with: One cheese toastie, please.

    Helpful clue: Order, ask about a service charge, then ask whether you need to leave a tip.

La Boqueria: Colour and Choice in Barcelona

La Boqueria sits on La Rambla in Barcelona.

It has served the city as a market since 1836, and today more than 200 traders work there.

Bright fruit and vegetable stalls stand beside sellers of olives and preserved foods.

Visitors can also find nuts and pulses, poultry and eggs, meat, fish and seafood.

Grocery stalls provide everyday ingredients, while small bars offer a place to stop and eat.

This mix makes La Boqueria more than a sightseeing stop: it is a working food market where visitors can compare fresh produce, specialist foods and ready-to-eat dishes.

Reading

Marché des Enfants Rouges: Old Paris, Many Flavours

Marché des Enfants Rouges is a small covered market in Paris.

Founded in 1615, it is the city's oldest covered food market.

Fresh produce and farm cheese share the space with counters serving ready-to-eat food.

A visitor might see chicken skewers, vegetable couscous or a Breton buckwheat galette.

Other choices include oysters and fresh fruit juice.

The prepared food comes from several food cultures, so a short walk can reveal very different flavours.

It is an easy place to choose a simple lunch while enjoying the close, historic market atmosphere.

Borough Market: Produce and Street Food in London

Borough Market has more than 100 stalls and shops in London.

They are spread across Three Crown Square, Green Market and Borough Market Kitchen.

Visitors can buy British seafood, regional cheese and cured meat, or stop for Middle Eastern meze, falafel or shawarma.

Cakes, pastries and bao buns add quick sweet and savoury choices.

The market works well for two different plans: shopping for ingredients to take home or choosing lunch and eating it nearby.

Moving through its three areas shows how many kinds of food one market can bring together.

Tipping in Spain, France and the UK

Tipping customs change between Spain, France and the UK.

At a simple market stall or self-service counter, people normally pay the displayed price unless the seller says otherwise.

In Spain, a tip is optional, and some people simply round up the bill.

In France, restaurant prices normally include service, so extra money is optional.

In the UK, a restaurant bill may already include an optional or required service charge.

A visitor should read the bill before adding more money.

The safest habit in all three countries is simple: check the bill, then ask.
